title: Network Delay Time
problem: There are n nodes labelled 1..n and a list of directed, weighted edges times[i] = [u, v, w] (a signal takes w time to go from u to v). A signal is sent from node k. Return the time it takes for all nodes to receive it, or -1 if some node can never receive it.
example: Explanation: From 2, node 1 and node 3 get the signal at time 1, node 4 at time 2. The last node hears it at
intuition: Every node receives the signal at its shortest-path distance from k. So the answer is simply "the maximum over all shortest distances from k ", and -1 if any distance is infinite.

All weights are non-negative, which is exactly Dijkstra's condition. Dijkstra greedily finalises the closest unfinished node: once you pop a node with distance d from a min-heap, no later path can be shorter, because every other path must go through a node at distance >= d and then add non-negative weights. Trace on the example: heap {(0,2)} → pop 2, push (1,1), (1,3) → pop 1 (no out-edges) → pop 3, push (2,4) → pop 4. Distances [1:1, 2:0, 3:1, 4:2], max is 2.
notes: Say it like this: "Each node hears the signal at its shortest distance from k, so I need single-source shortest paths and then the max. Bellman-Ford does it in O(V·E). Since weights are non-negative I use Dijkstra with a min- heap in O(E log V), and return -1 if any node stays at infinity."
Edge cases: node unreachable (return -1); n = 1 (answer 0); nodes are 1-indexed, so size arrays n + 1 and skip index 0 when taking the max.
Common mistakes: taking the max over index 0 (which is infinity); forgetting the stale-entry check (still correct but slower); using a visited set and also pushing duplicates inconsistently.
Follow-ups: "What if weights can be negative?" Dijkstra breaks; use Bellman-Ford. "Dense graph?" Array-based Dijkstra in O(V²) beats the heap version. 11.2
simple: A signal starts at node k and travels along weighted edges. When has it reached everyone?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Bellman-Ford: relax every edge again and again. After n-1 rounds every shortest path (which has at most n-1 edges) has been discovered.
steps: dist[k] = 0, everything else infinity.
Repeat n-1 times: for each edge (u, v, w), if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v]. Stop early if a round changes nothing.
Answer = max of dist, or -1 if any is infinity.
approaches.why: Up to n-1 rounds, each scanning all E edges; only the distance array is stored.
approaches.simple: Bellman-Ford: relax every edge n − 1 times.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Dijkstra with a min-heap of (distance, node).
steps: Build an adjacency list.
Push (0, k). Pop the smallest; if it is stale (d > dist[u]), skip it.
For each neighbour, if d + w improves dist[v], update and push.
Answer = max of dist (or -1).
approaches.time: O(E log E) (often written O(E log V))
approaches.why: Each edge can push one heap entry, and each heap operation costs log of the heap size; adjacency list and heap hold O(V + E). JavaScript has no built-in priority queue, so here is a small binary min-heap that compares arrays by their first element. Later questions today reuse this exact MinHeap class.
approaches.simple: Dijkstra: always expand the closest unfinished node using a min-heap. The answer is the largest final distance.

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
problem: You get a list of airline tickets [from, to]. All tickets belong to one traveller who starts at "JFK" and uses every ticket exactly once. Return the itinerary; if several are valid, return the one that is smallest in lexical order when read as a single sequence. At least one valid itinerary is guaranteed.
example: Explanation: ["JFK","SFO","ATL","JFK","ATL","SFO"] is also valid but is lexically larger.
intuition: Airports are nodes, tickets are directed edges, and "use every ticket exactly once" means we need an Eulerian path starting at JFK. Lexical order suggests always trying the smallest destination first.

Pure greedy (always take the smallest next airport) can get stuck: you might walk into a dead end while tickets remain. Hierholzer's trick fixes this: do DFS, always taking the smallest unused edge, and add an airport to the answer only after all its outgoing edges are used (post-order). The dead end gets appended first, so after reversing it lands at the end of the route, which is exactly where it must be. Each edge is used once, so it is linear (plus sorting).
notes: Say it like this: "Tickets are edges and I must use each exactly once, so this is an Eulerian path from JFK. Backtracking in sorted order works but is exponential. Hierholzer's algorithm does DFS taking the smallest edge first and appends a node only after its edges are exhausted, then reverses: O(E log E) for the sorting, linear after that."
Edge cases: duplicate tickets (same from/to twice) must both be used; airports with no outgoing tickets; a single ticket.

Common mistakes: plain greedy without post-order (gets stuck at a dead end like JFK -> KUL when JFK -> NRT -> JFK should come first); using a Set for destinations (loses duplicate tickets); forgetting to reverse.

Follow-ups: "Why does post-order work?" A node is appended only when it is stuck, and the only node that can get stuck is the true end of the remaining path, so it belongs at the end. "Very deep graph?" Convert to an iterative stack to avoid stack overflow. 11.3
simple: Use every ticket once to build the trip from JFK, choosing the alphabetically smallest route.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Backtracking: try destinations in sorted order, and undo when you get stuck.
steps: Build adjacency lists and sort each one.
DFS from JFK: for each unused ticket from the current airport (in sorted order), use it, recurse, and undo on failure.
The first path that uses all tickets is the lexically smallest one, because we tried choices in sorted order.
approaches.time: exponential in the worst case (O(E^d) where d is the max out-degree)
approaches.why: Backtracking may explore many partial routes before finding the full one; recursion depth and adjacency lists are O(E).
approaches.simple: Backtracking with sorted destinations, undoing when you get stuck.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Hierholzer's algorithm with min-ordered adjacency.
steps: For every airport keep its destinations in a min-heap (or a list sorted descending so the smallest pops from the end).
dfs(u): while u has unused tickets, pop the smallest destination v and dfs(v).
After the loop, add u to the front of the route (post-order).
The route built this way is the answer.
approaches.why: Sorting/heaping the destinations costs E log E; afterwards each ticket is popped exactly once. Adjacency, route and recursion stack are O(E).
approaches.simple: Hierholzer: always take the smallest next destination; when stuck, add the airport to the route. Reverse at the end.

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
problem: Given n points on a 2D plane, the cost of connecting two points is their Manhattan distance |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|. Return the minimum total cost to connect all points so that there is exactly one simple path between any two points.
intuition: "Connect everything with exactly one path between any two points and minimum total cost" is the definition of a Minimum Spanning Tree. The graph is complete: every pair of points has an edge, so there are about n²/2 edges.

Two classic MST algorithms: Kruskal sorts all edges and adds the cheapest one that does not create a cycle (needs DSU). Prim grows one tree, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it. On a complete (dense) graph, Prim with a plain array runs in O(n²) without even building the edge list, which beats sorting n² edges.
notes: Say it like this: "This is an MST on a complete graph. Kruskal over all n² edges works in O(n² log n) time and O(n²) space. Because the graph is dense, array-based Prim is better: O(n²) time, O(n) space, and I never build the edge list."
Edge cases: one point (cost 0); duplicate points (distance 0 edges are fine).
Common mistakes: using heap-Prim and pushing all n² edges (works but slower and uses more memory); summing minDist of a point that was already in the tree; using Euclidean distance.

Follow-ups: "Which MST algorithm when the graph is sparse?" Kruskal or heap-Prim, O(E log E). "Can you beat O(n²) for Manhattan MST?" Yes, there is an O(n log n) sweep that keeps only O(n) candidate edges, but it is rarely expected. 11.4
simple: Connect all points with the cheapest total cable (Manhattan distance).

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Kruskal on all pairs.
steps: Generate all n(n-1)/2 edges with their Manhattan cost.
Sort by cost.
Walk the edges; use DSU to add an edge only if it joins two different components. Stop after n-1 edges.
approaches.why: Sorting n² edges costs n² log(n²) = O(n² log n); the edge list itself is O(n²).
approaches.simple: Kruskal: make all edges, sort them, and add cheap ones that don't create a cycle.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Prim's algorithm with an array (no heap, no edge list).
steps: minDist[i] = cheapest known edge from the current tree to point i; start with point 0 at 0, the rest at infinity.
Repeat n times: pick the not-yet-added point with the smallest minDist (linear scan), add it to the tree and to the cost.
Update minDist[j] for every point j not in the tree using the distance to the newly added point.
approaches.why: n rounds, each doing an O(n) scan and an O(n) update; only two arrays of size n.
approaches.simple: Prim: grow one tree, each time adding the closest point not yet connected.

title: Swim In Rising Water
problem: You are given an n x n grid where grid[i][j] is the elevation of that cell (all values are a permutation of 0..n²-1). At time t the water level is t, and you can swim between 4-directionally adjacent cells only if both have elevation <= t. Swimming takes no time. Return the minimum time t at which you can get from (0,0) to (n-1,n-1).
example: Explanation: You cannot leave (0,0) until t = 1 or 2, and you cannot enter (1,1) until t = 3. At t = 3 every
intuition: For a fixed path, the time you need is the maximum elevation on that path. So we want the path from corner to corner whose maximum cell is as small as possible: a "minimax path".

Two observations each lead to a solution. (1) Feasibility is monotonic: if you can make it at time t, you can at t + 1. That gives a linear or binary search over t with a BFS check. (2) Dijkstra still works when the path cost is max instead of +, because extending a path never makes its cost smaller. So we run Dijkstra where the "distance" to a cell is the smallest possible maximum elevation to reach it, and we stop when we pop the target.
notes: Say it like this: "The time for a path is the max elevation on it, so I want the minimax path. Trying every t with BFS is O(n⁴); binary searching t is O(n² log n). The cleanest is Dijkstra with max instead of sum: pop the cell with the smallest required time, push neighbours with max(t, height), and return when the target pops. That is also O(n² log n)."
Edge cases: n = 1 (answer is grid[0][0]); the start cell itself is high, so the answer is at least grid[0][0]; the target is high.

Common mistakes: starting the answer at 0 and forgetting the start cell's height; returning when the target is pushed instead of popped (with the push-time-visited trick it happens to be fine here, but in standard Dijkstra it is wrong); adding heights instead of taking max.
Follow-ups: "Another approach?" Sort cells by height and add them one at a time with a DSU; the answer is the height at which (0,0) and (n-1,n-1) become connected. Same O(n² log n). 11.5
simple: Water rises over time; you can swim to cells no higher than the water. When can you reach the corner?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Try every time from small to large.
steps: Start t at max(grid[0][0], grid[n-1][n-1]) (you cannot do better than either corner).
For each t, BFS from (0,0) through cells with elevation <= t.
Return the first t for which the target is reached.
approaches.why: Up to n² values of t, each with an O(n²) BFS; the BFS uses a visited grid and queue.
approaches.simple: Try time t = start, t + 1, … and check reachability each time.

approaches.why: Each of the n² cells is pushed once, each heap operation is O(log n²) = O(log n). Same big-O as binary search, but one pass and no guessing; this is the answer interviewers expect.
approaches.simple: Dijkstra where the cost of a path is its highest cell; a min-heap always expands the lowest one.

title: Alien Dictionary
problem: An alien language uses lowercase English letters in an unknown order. You get a list of words that is sorted according to that alien order. Return any string containing every letter that appears in the words, ordered consistently with the alien order. If the input is invalid (no order can explain it), return "". (LeetCode 269. Striver/GFG's version gives N words and K letters and is guaranteed valid; the solution is the same.)
example: Explanation: "wrt" < "wrf" gives t < f; "wrf" < "er" gives w < e; "er" < "ett" gives r < t; "ett" < "rftt"
gives e < r. So w < e < r < t < f.
intuition: Compare each pair of adjacent words. The first position where they differ tells you one ordering fact: a[j] comes before b[j]. Nothing after that position tells you anything (just like "apple" < "b" says nothing about 'p' vs anything). These facts are directed edges between letters, and an order that respects all edges is a topological order. A cycle means the input is contradictory.
One special invalid case: a longer word appears before its own prefix, like ["abc", "ab"]. No ordering can make that sorted, so return "".
notes: Say it like this: "Adjacent words give me ordering edges from their first differing letter, and the answer is a topological order of letters. A naive 'find a letter with no incoming edges' loop is O(U³); Kahn's algorithm is linear in characters plus edges. A cycle, or a word appearing before its own prefix, means return empty."
Edge cases: single word (any order of its letters); prefix case ["abc","ab"] → ""; letters with no constraints must still appear; duplicate edges must not inflate in-degree.

Common mistakes: comparing every pair instead of adjacent pairs (unnecessary) or continuing past the first difference (wrong); forgetting letters that never appear in any edge; double-counting a repeated edge in indeg, which leaves a letter stuck forever.

Follow-ups: "Return the lexicographically smallest valid order?" Use a min-heap instead of a queue in Kahn's. "Detect if the order is unique?" It is unique iff the queue never holds more than one letter at a time. 11.6
simple: From words sorted in an alien language, work out the order of the letters.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Build the same letter graph, then do a naive topological sort.
steps: Mark which letters appear; for each adjacent pair add the edge from the first difference (or return "" on the prefix case).
Repeat: scan all letters for one that is present, unused, and has no incoming edge from an unused letter. Append it and mark used.
If no such letter exists while letters remain, there is a cycle → "".
approaches.time: O(C + U³) where C = total characters and U ≤ 26 is the number of distinct letters
approaches.why: Each of up to U picks scans U letters and checks U possible incoming edges; the adjacency matrix is U×U. With U ≤ 26 this is small, but it does not scale to big alphabets.
approaches.simple: Build letter rules from neighbouring words and repeatedly pick a letter that nothing must come before.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Kahn's algorithm (BFS topological sort) with in-degrees.
steps: Build the graph as above, counting indeg[v] once per distinct edge.
Queue every present letter with in-degree
Pop a letter, append it, decrement in-degrees of its neighbours, queue those that reach
If the result is shorter than the number of distinct letters, there was a cycle → "".
approaches.time: O(C + U + E) where C = total characters, E ≤ U² edges
approaches.why: Building edges reads every character once; Kahn's touches each letter and edge once.
approaches.simple: Build the rules as a graph and run Kahn's topological sort. A cycle or a bad prefix means no valid order.

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problem: There are n cities and directed flights [from, to, price]. Return the cheapest price from src to dst using at most k stops (that is, at most k + 1 flights). Return -1 if no such route exists.
example: Explanation: 0 -> 1 -> 3 costs 700 with 1 stop. 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 costs 400 but needs 2 stops.
intuition: Plain Dijkstra fails here: it keeps only the cheapest way to reach each city, but a cheaper-but-longer route might be useless because it burns too many stops, while a pricier route with fewer stops was the one we needed.

Bellman-Ford has a lovely property: after round i, dist[v] is the cheapest cost using at most i edges. So running exactly k + 1 rounds answers the question directly. The one trick: in each round, relax from a copy of the previous round's distances, otherwise a single round can chain several edges together and exceed the limit.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force DFS over routes with at most k+1 flights is exponential. Bellman-Ford after i rounds gives the cheapest cost using at most i edges, so k+1 rounds, each relaxing from a copy of the previous array, gives the answer in O(k·E) time and O(n) space."
Edge cases: src == dst (cost 0); k = 0 (only direct flights); no route at all (-1).

Common mistakes: relaxing in place (lets one round use several flights and breaks the stop limit); running k rounds instead of k + 1; using plain Dijkstra keyed only by cost and keeping one best per city.

Follow-ups: "Striver's version?" A BFS queue of (stops, node, cost) processed level by level, relaxing a node only if the cost improves; it is the same idea and also O(k·E). "Dijkstra version?" Make the state (city, stopsUsed) so you keep one best per pair. Shortest Path in Undirected 11.7
simple: Cheapest flight from src to dst with at most k stops.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: DFS over all routes with at most k + 1 flights.
steps: From src, try every outgoing flight, tracking cost and flights remaining.
Reaching dst updates the best answer.
Prune if no flights remain or the cost already exceeds the best. Avoid revisiting a city on the current path (positive prices make cycles useless).
approaches.why: Each level of recursion can branch to up to n cities, k + 1 levels deep; recursion depth is at most k + 2.
approaches.simple: Try every route recursively with a stops budget.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Bellman-Ford limited to k + 1 rounds.
steps: dist[src] = 0, others infinity.
Repeat k + 1 times: copy dist into next; for each flight (u, v, w) with dist[u] finite, set next[v] = min(next[v], dist[u] + w); then dist = next.
Return dist[dst] or -1.
approaches.why: k + 1 rounds over all E flights; two arrays of size n.
approaches.simple: Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds, using a copy of the previous round so each round adds at most one flight.

title: Shortest Path in Undirected Graph with Unit Weights
problem: You are given an undirected graph with n nodes (0..n-1) and m edges, where every edge has weight 1. Given a source src, return an array with the shortest distance from src to every node, using -1 for nodes that cannot be reached. (GFG "Shortest path in Undirected Graph having unit distance".)
example: Explanation: e.g. node 6 is reached by 0-1-2-6 (3 edges); node 8 by 0-1-2-6-8 (4 edges).
intuition: When every edge costs the same, "shortest path" means "fewest edges". BFS explores the graph in layers: first all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on. The first time BFS reaches a node is therefore via a shortest path, and we never need to update it again. No heap is needed, since the queue is already sorted by distance.
notes: Say it like this: "With unit weights, the shortest path is the one with fewest edges, which BFS finds layer by layer. Generic relaxation is O(V·E); BFS is O(V + E), and the first time a node is reached is final."
Edge cases: disconnected nodes (-1); src isolated; parallel edges or self-loops (harmless).
Common mistakes: marking visited when popping instead of when pushing (can push a node many times); forgetting to add both directions; using DFS (DFS does not give shortest paths).

Follow-ups: "Weights are only 0 or 1?" Use 0-1 BFS with a deque: push to the front on 0-edges, back on 1-edges. "Need the actual path?" Store parent[v] = u when you set dist[v] and walk back from the target. 11.8
simple: Shortest number of edges from the source to every node.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Generic relaxation (Bellman-Ford style), ignoring that weights are all
steps: dist[src] = 0, others infinity.
Up to n-1 rounds: for every edge, relax in both directions with cost
Stop when a round changes nothing.
Replace infinity with -1.
approaches.why: Up to n-1 rounds over m edges; only the distance array.
approaches.simple: Relax every edge over and over until nothing improves.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: BFS from the source.
steps: Build an adjacency list (add both directions).
dist[src] = 0, push src.
Pop u; for each neighbour v with dist[v] == -1, set dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 and push it.
approaches.why: Each node is enqueued once and each edge is looked at twice; adjacency list plus queue.
approaches.simple: BFS: when all edges cost 1, the order in which BFS reaches nodes is their distance order.

title: Shortest Path in DAG
problem: Given a weighted Directed Acyclic Graph with V nodes (0..V-1) and E edges [u, v, w], find the shortest distance from node 0 to every node. Use -1 for unreachable nodes. (GFG "Shortest path in Directed Acyclic Graph".)
example: Explanation: 0->4->2 costs 3 (better than 0->1->2 = 5); 0->4->5->3 costs 6 (better than via 2 = 9).
intuition: In a DAG there is a topological order in which every edge goes forward. If we process nodes in that order, by the time we reach node u, every edge coming into u has already been relaxed, so dist[u] is final. Then relaxing u 's outgoing edges once is enough. One pass over all edges, no heap, and it even works with negative weights (there can be no negative cycle in a DAG).
notes: Say it like this: "Bellman-Ford solves it in O(V·E). Because it is a DAG, I can process nodes in topological order: every incoming edge of a node is relaxed before the node itself, so one pass of relaxation finishes in O(V + E). It also handles negative weights."
Edge cases: nodes unreachable from 0 (-1), including nodes that come before 0 in topological order; a single node.

Common mistakes: relaxing from nodes whose dist is still infinity (overflow with int); starting topo sort only from node 0 and missing other zero in-degree nodes (fine for distances, but be consistent); using Dijkstra unnecessarily.

Follow-ups: "Longest path in a DAG?" Same algorithm with max (or negate weights); longest path is NP-hard in general graphs but linear in a DAG. "DFS topo instead of Kahn's?" Striver uses DFS with a stack; both are O(V + E). 11.9
simple: Shortest paths from node 0 in a graph with no cycles.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Bellman-Ford, which works on any graph without negative cycles.
steps: dist[0] = 0, others infinity.
Up to V-1 rounds of relaxing all edges, stopping early when nothing changes.
Map infinity to -1.
approaches.why: V-1 rounds over E edges; one distance array.
approaches.simple: Bellman-Ford style relaxing of every edge.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Topological order (Kahn's), then relax each node's edges once.
steps: Build adjacency list and in-degrees.
Get a topological order with Kahn's BFS.
dist[0] = 0; for each u in topo order with finite dist[u], relax every edge u -> v.
Map infinity to -1.
approaches.why: Topological sort and the relaxation pass each touch every node and edge once.
approaches.simple: Get a topological order, then relax edges in that order once. Each node's distance is final when you reach it.

title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
problem: Given an undirected, weighted graph with V vertices (0..V-1), edges [u, v, w] with non-negative weights, and a source src, return the shortest distance from src to every vertex. (GFG "Implementing Dijkstra Algorithm"; the graph is connected.)
example: Explanation: 2->1 costs 3; 2->1->0 costs 4, cheaper than the direct edge 2->0 of 6.
intuition: Dijkstra is BFS generalised to weighted edges. Keep tentative distances. Repeatedly take the unfinished vertex with the smallest tentative distance: that distance is final, because any other route to it would have to leave the finished set through some vertex that is already at least as far, and adding non-negative weights cannot make it shorter. Then relax its edges.

The only design question is how you find "the smallest unfinished vertex": a linear scan (O(V²) total) or a min-heap (O((V + E) log V)). Striver also shows a TreeSet version that deletes outdated entries; the heap with a stale check is simpler and just as fast.
notes: Say it like this: "Dijkstra greedily finalises the closest unfinished vertex, which is valid because weights are non- negative. With a linear scan it is O(V²), good for dense graphs; with a min-heap and lazy deletion of stale entries it is O((V + E) log V), good for sparse graphs."
Edge cases: unreachable vertices (decide what to return: infinity, -1, or 1e9 per the problem); self-loops; zero- weight edges are fine.

Common mistakes: using Dijkstra with negative weights (gives wrong answers silently); forgetting both directions for an undirected graph; comparator a[0] - b[0] overflowing with huge distances (use Integer.compare); not skipping stale entries (still correct, just slower).

Follow-ups: "Why not negative weights?" A finalised vertex could later be improved through a negative edge. "Print the path?" Keep a parent array, set when relaxing, and walk back from the target. "Priority queue vs set?" Set (TreeSet) lets you erase the old entry so the heap never holds duplicates; same complexity. 11.10
simple: Shortest paths from a source when all weights are non-negative.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Dijkstra with a linear scan instead of a heap.
steps: dist[src] = 0, others infinity; done[] all false.
Repeat V times: scan for the unfinished vertex u with the smallest dist; mark it done.
Relax all edges of u.
approaches.why: V rounds with an O(V) scan each, plus every edge relaxed once. This is actually the best choice for very dense graphs (E close to V²).
approaches.simple: Each round, scan for the closest unfinished node, finish it, and update its neighbours.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Dijkstra with a min-heap and lazy deletion.
steps: Push (0, src).
Pop (d, u); skip if d > dist[u] (stale).
For each edge u -> v with weight w, if d + w < dist[v], update and push (dist[v], v).
approaches.why: Each edge can cause one push, and a heap of at most E entries costs O(log E) = O(log V) per operation.
approaches.simple: Same idea but a min-heap gives the closest node quickly; skip outdated heap entries.

title: Path With Minimum Effort
pattern: Dijkstra on grid (minimise the maximum edge)
problem: You are given a rows x cols grid heights. You start at the top-left cell and want to reach the bottom-right cell, moving up, down, left or right. The effort of a route is the maximum absolute height difference between two consecutive cells on it. Return the minimum effort needed.
example: Explanation: Route 1 -> 3 -> 5 -> 3 -> 5 has differences 2,2,2,2, so effort 2. Every other route has a jump
intuition: This is the edge-weighted cousin of Swim in Rising Water. The edge between two neighbouring cells has weight |h1 - h2|, and a route costs the max edge on it, not the sum. We want the route with the smallest max.

Dijkstra still works with max: extending a route can only keep or increase its cost, so the first time we pop a cell from the min-heap, its cost is optimal. dist[r][c] = smallest effort found so far to reach (r, c). Alternatively, effort feasibility is monotonic ("can I do it with effort ≤ E?"), so binary search + BFS also works.
notes: Say it like this: "Cells are nodes, the edge weight is the height difference, and a path costs its maximum edge. DFS over all paths is exponential; binary search on the effort with BFS is O(RC log H). Dijkstra with max instead of plus is O(RC log RC) and is the standard answer."
Edge cases: 1x1 grid (answer 0); a single row or column (answer is the max adjacent difference); all heights equal (0).

Common mistakes: summing differences instead of taking the max; returning when the target is pushed rather than popped; marking visited on push (wrong here because arriving from a different neighbour can give a smaller edge).
Follow-ups: "DSU alternative?" Sort all edges by weight and union them in order until start and end are connected; the last weight added is the answer (Kruskal-style), O(RC log RC). 11.11
simple: Find a path where the biggest height jump between neighbours is as small as possible.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Try every simple path with DFS and backtracking.
steps: DFS from (0,0), keeping the max difference seen on the current path and an on-path marker.
When reaching the target, update the best answer.
Prune when the current effort already reaches the best answer.
approaches.why: The number of simple paths in a grid explodes; recursion depth and the on-path grid are O(rows · cols). Only usable on tiny grids.
approaches.simple: Explore every path with DFS, tracking its biggest jump.

title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
problem: Given a directed, weighted graph with V vertices and edges [u, v, w] (weights may be negative) and a source src, return the shortest distance from src to every vertex. Use 100000000 (1e8) for unreachable vertices. If the graph contains a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source, return [-1]. (GFG "Bellman-Ford".)
intuition: Dijkstra fails with negative edges because it finalises a vertex too early. Bellman-Ford finalises nothing; it just keeps relaxing every edge. Why V-1 rounds? A shortest path without cycles has at most V-1 edges, and after round i every shortest path that uses at most i edges is correct (each round extends correct paths by at least one more edge). Negative cycle detection follows directly: after V-1 rounds all distances should be final. If one more round can still improve something, there is a cycle whose total weight is negative, and you can go around it forever.
There is no faster algorithm for general graphs with negative weights in an interview setting, so both approaches below are Bellman-Ford; the optimised one stops as soon as a round changes nothing.
notes: Say it like this: "Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V-1 times, because a shortest simple path has at most V-1 edges. If a V-th round still improves a distance, there is a negative cycle. It is O(V·E); I add an early exit when a round changes nothing, which is the same worst case but much faster in practice."
Edge cases: unreachable vertices stay at 1e8; a negative cycle that is not reachable from src should not trigger [-1] (the dist[u]!= INF check guarantees this); V = 1.

Common mistakes: relaxing from an unreachable vertex (INF + negative looks smaller than INF and corrupts results); running only V-2 rounds; treating an undirected edge with negative weight as two directed edges (that is itself a negative cycle).

Follow-ups: "Why use it over Dijkstra?" Negative weights and cycle detection, or when you need "at most k edges" (see 11.6). "Faster in practice?" SPFA (queue-based Bellman-Ford) only re-relaxes vertices whose distance changed; same worst case. 11.12
simple: Shortest paths that work even with negative edges, and detect negative cycles.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Textbook Bellman-Ford with all V-1 rounds every time.
steps: dist[src] = 0, others 1e8.
Exactly V-1 rounds: relax every edge (skip if dist[u] is 1e8).
One extra round: if any edge still relaxes, return [-1].
approaches.why: V rounds (V-1 plus the check) over E edges, always, even if the answer stabilises early.
approaches.simple: Relax every edge exactly V − 1 times.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Bellman-Ford with early termination.
steps: Run up to V rounds. In each, relax all edges and remember whether anything changed.
If a round changes nothing, distances are final and no negative cycle is reachable: return.
If the V -th round still changes something, return [-1].
approaches.time: O(V · E) worst case, often far less in practice
approaches.why: Worst case is still V rounds, but on typical graphs distances settle after a few rounds.
approaches.simple: Relax in rounds and stop early when nothing changes. Still changing in round V means a negative cycle.

title: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm
pattern: All-pairs shortest paths (DP over intermediate vertices)
problem: You are given an n x n adjacency matrix dist of a directed weighted graph, where dist[i][j] is the edge weight from i to j, dist[i][i] = 0, and 1e8 (100000000) means there is no edge. Modify the matrix in place so that dist[i][j] becomes the shortest distance from i to j (still 1e8 if unreachable). (GFG "Floyd Warshall"; older versions use -1 for "no edge", in which case convert -1 to infinity first and back at the end.)
intuition: Think DP: let d_k[i][j] be the shortest path from i to j that is only allowed to pass through intermediate vertices 0..k. When we allow vertex k too, the best path either avoids k (cost d_{k-1}[i][j]) or goes through it once (cost d_{k-1}[i][k] + d_{k-1}[k][j]). Take the minimum. After allowing all vertices, we have the true shortest paths.
The k loop must be the outermost loop; that is the whole trick. Updating in place is safe because row k and column k do not change during iteration k (dist[k][k] is 0).
notes: Say it like this: "Running Bellman-Ford from every vertex gives all pairs in O(V²·E), up to O(V⁴). Floyd-Warshall is a DP over which vertices may be used as intermediates: with k outermost, dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]), O(V³) time and in place. A negative dist[i][i] reveals a negative cycle."
Edge cases: unreachable pairs stay INF; self-distance 0; negative edges are fine, negative cycles make results meaningless (detect via the diagonal).
Common mistakes: putting k as the inner loop (wrong answer); adding INF + INF or INF + w (overflow or fake paths, so skip INF); forgetting to convert -1 to INF in the old GFG version.

Follow-ups: "When prefer it over V × Dijkstra?" Small dense graphs (V up to ~400) or negative edges; V × Dijkstra is O(V·E log V), better for large sparse graphs with non-negative weights. "Reconstruct paths?" Keep next[i] [j] updated alongside dist. "City with the smallest number of neighbours within threshold" (LeetCode 1334) is a direct application. 11.13
simple: Shortest paths between every pair of nodes.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Run a single-source algorithm from every vertex. Weights may be negative, so the safe choice is Bellman-Ford.
steps: Turn the matrix into an edge list.
For each source s, run Bellman-Ford and record the row.
Copy all rows back into the matrix.
approaches.time: O(V² · E), which is O(V⁴) for a dense matrix
approaches.why: V runs of an O(V·E) algorithm; the result matrix and edge list are O(V²).
approaches.simple: Run a single-source algorithm from every node.

approaches.label: Optimal

steps: For k from 0 to n-1 (outermost), for every i, for every j:
If dist[i][k] and dist[k][j] are both finite, dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]).
(Optional) If any dist[i][i] < 0 afterwards, there is a negative cycle.
approaches.why: Three nested loops over V; the update happens in the given matrix.
approaches.simple: Floyd-Warshall: for each middle node k, check whether going i → k → j beats the current i → j.

title: Word Ladder II
problem: Given beginWord, endWord and a dictionary wordList, a transformation sequence changes one letter at a time, and every intermediate word (and endWord) must be in the dictionary. Return all shortest transformation sequences from beginWord to endWord, each as a list of words. Return an empty list if none exists.
example: Explanation: Both sequences have 5 words, and no shorter sequence exists.
intuition: Words are nodes; two words are connected if they differ in exactly one letter. Shortest sequences in an unweighted graph means BFS. The twist is that we need all shortest paths, not just the length.

Two rules make it work. First, a word may be used by several paths on the same level (both "dot" and "lot" could lead to the same next word), so only delete words from the dictionary after the whole level is processed. Second, storing full paths in the queue (Striver's first version) copies lists constantly and blows up on big tests. The efficient way: BFS only records each word's depth, then a DFS walks backwards from endWord, stepping only to words whose depth is exactly one less. Every such backward walk is guaranteed to reach beginWord along a shortest path, so the DFS never wastes work on dead ends.
notes: Say it like this: "It is BFS on a word graph, but I need all shortest paths. Storing full paths in the queue works but copies lists and can be exponential. Instead I BFS once to get each word's depth, then DFS backwards from endWord, only stepping to words exactly one level shallower, so every branch of the DFS produces an answer."
Edge cases: endWord not in the dictionary (return []); beginWord inside the dictionary (remove it so it is not revisited); no path exists.

Common mistakes: deleting a word from the dictionary as soon as one path uses it inside the same level in the path-BFS (loses other shortest paths); DFS forward from beginWord using depths (explores dead ends and TLEs); not stopping BFS at endWord's level.

Follow-ups: "Only the length?" That is Word Ladder I: plain BFS, O(N · L² · 26). "Speed up further?" Bidirectional BFS from both ends, meeting in the middle, cuts the explored frontier dramatically. 11.14
simple: List every shortest transformation chain from start word to end word.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: BFS over whole paths.
steps: Queue holds paths, starting with [beginWord].
Process level by level. For each path, try every one-letter change of its last word; if the new word is in the dictionary, enqueue the extended path and remember the word as "used this level".
After the level, remove all used words from the dictionary. If any path ended at endWord on this level, stop and return those paths.
approaches.time: O(P · L · 26 · L) where P = number of partial paths explored (can be exponential)
approaches.why: Every partial path is copied and stored; each expansion tries 26·L changes, each building an L-length string.
approaches.simple: BFS that carries whole paths, keeping the ones that reach the end first.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: BFS for depths, then backward DFS.
steps: BFS from beginWord, recording depth[word] the first time each word is reached (remove it from the dictionary when it gets its depth). Stop once endWord is dequeued.
If endWord has no depth, return [].
DFS from endWord: from word w at depth d, try every one-letter change p; if depth[p] == d - 1, prepend p and recurse. When you reach beginWord, record a copy of the path.
approaches.time: O(N · L · 26 · L + S · K) where N = dictionary size, L = word length, S = number of answers, K = path length
approaches.why: BFS generates 26·L neighbours for each word, each costing O(L) to build/hash; the backward DFS only walks edges that lie on shortest paths, so it is proportional to the output size. The depth map stores each word once.
approaches.simple: BFS to record each word's level, then walk back from the end word only through words one level lower.

title: Disjoint Set (Union-Find)
problem: Design a data structure over n elements (1..n here) that supports two operations: union(u, v) merges the groups containing u and v, and find(u) returns the representative (root) of u 's group, so find(u) == find(v) tells you whether u and v are connected. (GFG "Disjoint set (Union-Find)"; Striver teaches union by rank and union by size.)
example: Explanation: After the first five unions the groups are {1,2,3} and {4,5,6,7}, so 3 and 7 are not connected
intuition: Represent each group as a tree in a parent[] array; the root is the group's representative. find walks up to the root; union hangs one root under the other.

Done naively, trees can become long chains (union 1-2, 2-3, 3-4,... makes a linked list), so find costs O(n). Two small fixes make it almost O(1): - Union by rank/size: always attach the shorter (or smaller) tree under the taller (or bigger) one, so height stays O(log n). - Path compression: while finding the root, point every visited node directly at the root, so later finds are one hop.

Together, operations cost O(α(n)) amortised, where α is the inverse Ackermann function, at most 4 for any realistic n. "Size" is often more useful than "rank" because it also tells you the size of each component (used in 11.18).
notes: Say it like this: "A DSU keeps each group as a tree in a parent array. Naively find can be O(n) on a chain. With union by rank or size plus path compression, each operation is O(α(n)) amortised, effectively constant. I return a boolean from union so callers can tell whether it merged two groups or found a cycle."
Edge cases: union of an element with itself; 0- vs 1-indexed nodes (allocate n + 1); calling find before any union (each node is its own root).

Common mistakes: comparing parent[u] == parent[v] instead of find(u) == find(v) (parents are not necessarily roots); updating rank/size on the child instead of the root; increasing rank when ranks differ.

Follow-ups: "Why not just DFS each query?" DFS is O(V + E) per query and does not handle edges arriving over time; DSU handles dynamic connectivity incrementally. "Can DSU delete edges?" Not directly; process offline in reverse or use more advanced structures. "Recursion depth of find?" With union by rank it is O(log n); an iterative two-pass find avoids recursion entirely. 11.15
simple: Keep track of groups as you join items, and answer "are these two in the same group?" quickly.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Plain parent array without any balancing. 1. parent[i] = i. 2. find(x): follow parent until parent[x] == x.
steps: union(u, v): find both roots; if different, set parent[rootV] = rootU.
approaches.time: O(n) per operation in the worst case
approaches.why: Without balancing, a chain of n nodes can form, so find walks O(n) links.
approaches.simple: Each item points to a parent; follow parents to the leader. Joining links one leader under the other.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Path compression plus union by rank or by size (both shown; use one).
steps: find(x): if x is not a root, set parent[x] = find(parent[x]) and return it.
unionByRank(u, v): attach the root with smaller rank under the other; if ranks are equal, pick one and increase its rank.
unionBySize(u, v): attach the root with smaller size under the other and add the sizes.
approaches.why: Balancing keeps trees shallow and path compression flattens them further; arrays of size n for parent, rank and size.
approaches.simple: Add path compression (point straight to the leader after a search) and union by rank/size to keep trees flat.

title: Find the MST Weight
problem: Given a connected, undirected, weighted graph with V vertices (0..V-1) and edges [u, v, w], return the total weight of its Minimum Spanning Tree: a subset of V-1 edges that connects all vertices with the minimum possible total weight. (GFG "Minimum Spanning Tree".)
example: Explanation: Pick edges 0-2 (1) and 1-2 (3). Total 4. Edge 0-1 (5) would only add cost.
intuition: Both MST algorithms rely on the cut property: for any split of the vertices into two groups, the cheapest edge crossing the split is safe to include in some MST.

Prim grows one tree from a start vertex. The "split" is tree vs. not-tree, so it always adds the cheapest edge leaving the tree. A min-heap of (weight, vertex) finds it quickly. Kruskal goes the other way: sort all edges by weight and add each one unless it connects two vertices already in the same component. "Same component?" is exactly what the DSU from 11.14 answers in almost O(1).
Prim fits adjacency lists and dense graphs; Kruskal fits edge lists, which is what we are given.
notes: Say it like this: "MST relies on the cut property. Array-based Prim is O(V²); heap-based Prim is O(E log E); Kruskal sorts the edges and adds each one that joins two different DSU components, also O(E log E) but simplest when edges come as a list."

Edge cases: V = 1 (weight 0); parallel edges (keep the cheapest, which Kruskal and heap-Prim do automatically); self-loops (DSU rejects them); disconnected graph (no spanning tree; return -1 or a spanning forest weight, per the problem).

Common mistakes: in heap-Prim, marking a vertex as in the tree when pushing instead of when popping (adds the wrong edge); in Kruskal, not checking the cycle condition; using Dijkstra's dist + w instead of just w in Prim.

Follow-ups: "Print the MST edges?" In Kruskal record each accepted edge; in Prim also push the parent with each heap entry. "Is the MST unique?" Yes if all weights are distinct. "Second-best MST?" Try removing each MST edge and recomputing, or use max-edge-on-path queries. Number of Operations 11.16
simple: Find the total weight of the minimum spanning tree.

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Prim's algorithm with a linear scan (no heap).
steps: Build an adjacency matrix keeping the minimum weight for each pair (handles parallel edges).
key[0] = 0, others infinity. Repeat V times: pick the non-tree vertex with the smallest key, add it, add its key to the total.
Update key[v] for every non-tree neighbour from the matrix.
approaches.why: V rounds with O(V) scans and updates; the matrix is V×V. Fine for dense graphs, wasteful for sparse ones.
approaches.simple: Prim with a matrix: each round, scan for the cheapest edge out of the tree.

approaches.label: Better
approaches.lead: Prim's algorithm with a min-heap (Striver's main version).
steps: Build an adjacency list. Push (0, 0).
Pop (w, u). If u is already in the tree, skip. Otherwise add it and add w to the total.
Push (weight, v) for every neighbour v not yet in the tree.
approaches.why: Every edge can be pushed once from each side; each heap operation is O(log E).
approaches.simple: Prim with a min-heap of edges leaving the tree.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: Kruskal's algorithm with the DSU from 11.14.
steps: Sort edges by weight.
For each edge (u, v, w): if find(u)!= find(v), union them and add w.
Stop after V-1 edges.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the E DSU operations are O(E · α(V)). Same big-O as heap-Prim, but it works directly on the given edge list, needs no adjacency list, and the DSU is reusable. That simplicity is why it is the go-to when edges are given as a list.
approaches.simple: Kruskal: sort edges, add each one that joins two different groups (Union-Find).

title: Number of Operations to Make Network Connected
problem: There are n computers (0..n-1) and a list of cables connections[i] = [a, b]. In one operation you can unplug any existing cable and plug it between any two computers. Return the minimum number of operations to make all computers connected, or -1 if it is impossible.
example: Explanation: Computer 3 is isolated. Cable 1-2 is redundant (0,1,2 are already connected through 0), so move
intuition: Two facts settle the problem: 1. Connecting n computers needs at least n - 1 cables. If there are fewer, return -1 no matter what. 2. If there are enough cables, the redundant ones (cables inside an already-connected group) can always be moved. With c components you need exactly c - 1 moves, one to join each extra component. So the answer is just "number of components minus one", after the cable count check. Counting components is either DFS/BFS or DSU (start with n components, each successful union removes one).
notes: Say it like this: "We need at least n-1 cables, otherwise -1. If we have enough, every extra component costs exactly one move, so the answer is components minus one. DFS counting is O(n + E); DSU does it in one pass over the cables with near-constant operations and also counts redundant cables directly."
Edge cases: n = 1 (0 moves); no cables and n > 1 (-1); already connected (0).
Common mistakes: returning the number of redundant cables instead of components - 1; forgetting the -1 case; counting components but not checking the cable total.

Follow-ups: "Which cables should be moved?" Exactly the ones where union returned false. "Cables arrive over time and you must answer after each?" DSU handles that incrementally; DFS would have to rerun. 11.17
simple: Move cables so all computers are connected. How many moves are needed?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Count components with DFS.
steps: If connections.length < n - 1, return -1.
Build an adjacency list; DFS from every unvisited computer, counting how many times you start a new DFS.
Return components - 1.
approaches.why: Each computer and cable is visited once; the adjacency list stores every cable twice. (Already linear; the DSU version is the "Striver" answer and avoids building an adjacency list.)
approaches.simple: If there are fewer than n − 1 cables it's impossible; otherwise count groups with DFS and answer groups − 1.

approaches.label: Optimal
approaches.lead: DSU: count components and redundant cables in one pass.
steps: Start with components = n, extra = 0.
For each cable, if union(a, b) succeeds, components--; otherwise it is redundant, extra++.
If extra >= components - 1, return components - 1, else -1.
approaches.why: One near-constant DSU operation per cable; only the parent and size arrays, no adjacency list.
approaches.simple: Union-Find: count groups as cables are added; the answer is groups − 1 (if enough cables).

title: Number of Islands II
problem: You have an m x n grid that starts as all water. You are given a list of positions; for each [r, c] you turn that cell into land. After each operation, report the number of islands (groups of land cells connected 4-directionally). Return the list of counts. (LeetCode 305, premium; same as GFG/Striver "Number of Islands" with operators.)
example: Explanation: (0,0) makes 1 island; (0,1) joins it; (1,2) is separate (2 islands); (2,1) is separate (3
intuition: Recounting islands from scratch after every addition repeats almost all the work. Notice what one addition can do: it creates one new island, and then it can merge with up to 4 neighbouring islands, each merge reducing the count by one. That is exactly DSU's job.

Map cell (r, c) to id r * n + c. When a cell becomes land: count++, then for each land neighbour, if union actually merges two different sets, count--. If the same cell is added twice, nothing changes.
notes: Say it like this: "Recounting with BFS after each addition is O(k·m·n). Adding one cell creates one island and can merge with up to four neighbours, so I keep a DSU over cell ids: count++ for the new cell and count-- for every union that actually merges. That is O(mn + k·α) overall."
Edge cases: the same position added twice (must not increment); a cell whose neighbours belong to the same island (union returns false the second time, so count drops only once); 1x1 grid.
Common mistakes: decrementing for every land neighbour instead of only successful unions; id formula r * m + c instead of r * n + c; forgetting the duplicate check.

Follow-ups: "Cells can also turn back into water?" DSU cannot split sets; process the operations offline in reverse (removals become additions) or recount locally. "Very large sparse grid?" Use a HashMap for parent instead of an m*n array. 11.18
simple: Land is added cell by cell. After each addition, how many islands are there?

approaches.label: Brute Force
approaches.lead: Recount after every addition.
steps: Keep a boolean grid.
For each position, mark it as land, then count islands with BFS over the whole grid.
Record the count.
approaches.time: O(k · m · n) where k = number of positions
approaches.why: Each of the k recounts scans and BFSes the full grid.
approaches.simple: After each addition, count islands from scratch with BFS.

title: Making A Large Island
pattern: DSU with component sizes (or island labelling)
problem: You are given an n x n binary grid. You may change at most one 0 into a 1. Return the size of the largest island (4-directionally connected 1s) after the change.
example: Explanation: Flip either 0 to 1; it connects both single-cell islands, giving an island of size 3.
intuition: Flipping a zero joins that cell with all islands touching it. So its new island size is 1 + sum of sizes of the DISTINCT islands among its 4 neighbours. "Distinct" matters: two neighbours may belong to the same island, and counting it twice would be wrong.

So precompute, for every land cell, which island it belongs to and how big that island is. A DSU with sizes does exactly that (union all adjacent land cells, then find gives the island id and size[root] its size). Then each zero is a constant-time check of 4 neighbours. Remember the grid might have no zero at all, so also consider the biggest existing island.
notes: Say it like this: "Flipping each zero and running BFS is O(n⁴). Instead I build islands once with a DSU that tracks sizes. A flipped zero creates an island of 1 plus the sizes of the distinct islands around it, which I get from up to four find calls. Total O(n²·α). I also take the largest existing island, for the all-ones case."
Edge cases: all ones (answer n²); all zeros (answer 1); a zero surrounded by the same island on several sides (count it once).
Common mistakes: adding the same island's size twice; forgetting the no-zero case (answer would wrongly be 0); using size[cell] instead of size[find(cell)].

Follow-ups: "Without DSU?" DFS-label each island with an id (2, 3,...) and store area[id]; then the same per- zero check. Same complexity. "Flip up to k zeros?" No longer a local check; it becomes a much harder search problem.
simple: Change at most one 0 to 1. What is the biggest island you can get?

steps: For each 0 cell: set it to 1, BFS from it to measure its island, set it back.
Track the maximum.
If there was no zero, the answer is n * n.
approaches.why: Up to n² zeros, each followed by a BFS over up to n² cells.

steps: Union every land cell with its land neighbours (right and down are enough). Track the largest component size.

approaches.why: Each cell is unioned with at most two neighbours and each zero looks at 4 neighbours; DSU arrays have n² entries.
